confidence_note: The book's text was not available; facts come from a single summary preview (Shortform). The old text's claim that objections are a sign of interest, its quotation and the real-objection-versus-excuse split could not be found in any source and were dropped; the book's documented treatment of 'no' is the fear of rejection, so the story is re-grounded there. The 10 percent earnings figure is the summary's report of the book's claim, with no named study. Publication year follows the library record (2006).
facts: A summary calls the fear of rejection the main fear holding salespeople back; it is triggered by possible disapproval, judgment or rudeness.

Getting an appointment usually requires cold calling, which the book describes as the most stressful and least-liked part of selling; it treats prospecting as a learnable skill and advises preparing answers to common objections in advance.

Three ways to overcome the fear: rejection is not personal and is an expected, normal part of sales; courage takes practice and strengthens with use like a muscle; positive self-talk helps, for example repeating upbeat lines such as 'I'm doing great! I love my work!'.

Self-concept (how you see yourself and your skills) shapes attitude; a positive attitude helps customers respond more warmly, makes you enjoy and practise sales tasks more, and raises your earnings comfort zone. People tend to earn within about 10% of what they believe they are worth (a self-described $50,000 person earns roughly that).

The book opens by counting: the top 20% of salespeople earn about 80% of the profession's money; a winning edge is a small, steady advantage in skill, like a horse that wins by a nose and collects ten times the prize of second place.

tension: The step that starts every sale, asking, is the one most salespeople like least.
opening_idea: Open on cold calling as the most stressful and least-liked part of selling.

lessons.idea: Treat an expected 'no' as part of the job and let courage grow by use, instead of waiting until the dread has passed.
lessons.anchor: Rejection is not personal; courage is a muscle.
lessons.example: A freelancer who has put off phoning prospective clients makes the first call and finds the next easier.

reflect_final: What is one call, message or request you keep putting off because of how it might be received?

use_cases.situation: You keep postponing a call you are nervous about.
use_cases.move: Remind yourself a 'no' is normal and not a verdict on you, make the call, and note how it went.

use_cases.situation: A colleague dreads asking a client for an appointment.
use_cases.move: Say it is the least-liked part for most people and prepare an answer to a common objection together.

use_cases.situation: A friend who just started selling is discouraged after rejections.
use_cases.move: Share Tracy's view that rejection isn't personal and courage grows with practice, then ask which call went best.

pocket_idea: Rejection is an expected part of asking; courage grows with use like a muscle, so ask once more.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: In Tracy's book the hardest part of selling is the cold call, and the cure for dreading it is more calls.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Tracy names fear of rejection as the main thing holding salespeople back: cold calling is the most stressful, least-liked part. His remedy is three things: rejection is not personal, courage grows with practice like a muscle, and upbeat self-talk helps.
